On May 7th, a federal panel recommended a fundamental change to how the country handles disasters: push the money and the management down to the states, and shrink FEMA into a "payer of last resort."

In South Mississippi, we don't have to imagine what that means. We lived through Hurricane Katrina. Picture that recovery without the federal help that showed up for it.
What's on the table: raising the bar to even qualify for a federal disaster declaration, which by the report's own estimate could mean about 16 fewer major declarations a year, with moderate storms left entirely to the states. Moving flood insurance toward the private market, here on the Gulf Coast. Replacing the program that reimburses local governments with a block grant the state controls.
Putting the most risk on rural and under-resourced counties, if the state doesn't fill the gap. 

We've already seen what happens when federal dollars meant for Mississippi families don't reach them. Federal oversight isn't red tape down here. It's the safeguard that gets help to the people who need it.

It's time to improve outcomes for America's children. Let's do it together.

SECTION 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.

(a) Findings. Congress finds the following:

(1) The security of the United States border is a fundamental responsibility of the Federal Government under Article IV, Section 4 of the Constitution.

(2) Unprecedented levels of illegal immigration, fentanyl trafficking, and transnational gang activity have resulted in thousands of American deaths annually, strained public resources, and eroded community safety, particularly in border States and districts like Texas’s 20th Congressional District.

(3) American families have the right to raise their children in environments free from violence, exploitation, and ideological indoctrination that undermines parental authority and traditional values.

(4) Law enforcement officers, first responders, and veterans who have sacrificed for this Nation deserve unwavering support and protection from both physical threats and bureaucratic neglect.

(5) The right of law-abiding citizens to keep and bear arms, as guaranteed by the Second Amendment, must be vigorously protected against Federal overreach.

(6) Effective protection requires accountability, transparency, and the prioritization of American citizens and legal residents.

(b) Purpose. The purpose of this Act is to deliver decisive, comprehensive protections to American families and communities through strengthened borders, restored law and order, child safety measures, veteran support, and constitutional safeguards.

SECTION 3. DEFINITIONS.

In this Act:

The term “alien” has the meaning given to such term in section 101(a)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
The term “criminal gang” includes organizations designated under section 110 of title 18, United States Code, or successor provisions.

The term “parental rights” includes the fundamental right to direct the upbringing, education, and moral instruction of one’s children, as recognized by the Supreme Court.

Additional terms shall be defined consistent with existing Federal statutes.

TITLE I: BORDER SECURITY AND INTERIOR ENFORCEMENT

SEC. 101. COMPLETION OF PHYSICAL BORDER BARRIER.

The Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of Defense, shall complete construction of not fewer than 700 miles of reinforced physical barriers, sensors, and surveillance technology along the southern border within 24 months of enactment. Priority shall be given to high-traffic smuggling zones.

SEC. 102. MANDATORY DETENTION AND EXPEDITED REMOVAL.

All aliens apprehended after unlawful entry shall be detained pending removal or credible fear determination. Expedited removal procedures under section 235(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act shall be expanded to apply nationwide.

SEC. 103. PROHIBITION ON CATCH-AND-RELEASE.

No alien shall be released into the interior of the United States pending adjudication of immigration status unless the alien demonstrates lawful presence and passes comprehensive background checks. Release shall require approval by the Attorney General.

SEC. 104. PENALTIES FOR ILLEGAL REENTRY AND SMUGGLING.

Section 276 of the Immigration and Nationality Act is amended to impose a mandatory minimum sentence of 5 years for illegal reentry after prior removal, with enhanced penalties for those involved in smuggling or trafficking.

SEC. 105. DESIGNATION OF CARTELS AS TERRORIST ORGANIZATIONS.

Not later than 90 days after enactment, the Secretary of State shall designate major Mexican and Central American drug cartels and transnational criminal organizations as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, enabling full application of counterterrorism authorities.

SEC. 106. E-VERIFY MANDATE AND WORKPLACE ENFORCEMENT.

All employers with more than 10 employees shall utilize the E-Verify system. Civil and criminal penalties for knowingly employing unauthorized aliens are increased.

TITLE II: LAW AND ORDER AND PUBLIC SAFETY

SEC. 201. RESTORATION OF MANDATORY MINIMUMS.

Mandatory minimum sentences are reinstated for Federal crimes involving violence, firearms, fentanyl distribution resulting in death, and repeat serious offenders.

SEC. 202. SUPPORT FOR STATE AND LOCAL LAW ENFORCEMENT.

$5,000,000,000 is authorized for Byrne JAG and COPS grants to hire officers, acquire equipment, and support training, with eligibility conditioned on full cooperation with Federal immigration detainers.

SEC. 203. TRANSNATIONAL GANG TASK FORCES.

The Attorney General shall establish permanent multi-jurisdictional task forces targeting MS-13, Tren de Aragua, and similar gangs, with enhanced RICO and conspiracy penalties.

SEC. 204. PROTECTION OF SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS.

No Federal funds may be used for national firearms registration, red-flag confiscations without full due process (including notice, hearing, and counsel), or any infringement on the rights of law-abiding citizens.

SEC. 205. PENALTIES FOR ATTACKS ON LAW ENFORCEMENT.

Assaults on Federal, State, or local law enforcement officers resulting in serious injury shall carry a mandatory minimum of 10 years imprisonment.

TITLE III: CHILD AND FAMILY PROTECTION

SEC. 301. SCHOOL SAFETY AND PARENTAL NOTIFICATION.

All public schools receiving Federal funds shall implement immediate parental notification protocols for any violent incident, threat, or disciplinary action involving a child. Hardened school security grants are authorized, prioritizing resource officers.

SEC. 302. SAFEGUARDING CHILDREN FROM EXPLOITATION.

Federal education funds are withheld from States that permit the exposure of minors to sexually explicit content or gender ideology instruction without explicit, informed parental consent. Parental rights to opt out and review curriculum are guaranteed.

SEC. 303. ENHANCED PENALTIES FOR CHILD TRAFFICKING AND EXPLOITATION.

Mandatory minimum sentences of 25 years to life imprisonment are established for aggravated child sex trafficking, online enticement, and related offenses under chapters 77 and 110 of title 18, United States Code.

SEC. 304. FAMILY UNITY IN IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT.

Priority in removal proceedings shall be given to aliens with criminal records or recent unlawful entry, while protecting the unity of United States citizen families.

TITLE IV: VETERANS AND FIRST RESPONDERS PROTECTION

SEC. 401. EXPEDITED VETERANS’ BENEFITS AND HEALTHCARE.

The Department of Veterans Affairs shall prioritize claims processing for combat veterans and those with service-connected disabilities, with full benefits extended to training and deployment-related conditions.

SEC. 402. ANTI-FRAUD MEASURES FOR VETERANS PROGRAMS.

Criminal penalties are increased for benefits fraud, and a dedicated Inspector General task force is established.

SEC. 403. SUPPORT FOR FIRST RESPONDERS.

Tax credits, enhanced workers’ compensation, and mental health resources are authorized for law enforcement officers, firefighters, and emergency medical personnel injured or traumatized in the line of duty.

TITLE V: ENFORCEMENT AND OVERSIGHT

SEC. 501. REPORTING REQUIREMENTS.

The Secretary of Homeland Security and Attorney General shall submit quarterly reports to Congress detailing border encounters, removal statistics, crime reductions, and fund utilization.

SEC. 502. ACCOUNTABILITY PROVISIONS.

Federal officials who knowingly violate detention or enforcement provisions shall be subject to disciplinary action and loss of qualified immunity in appropriate cases.

SEC. 503. SEVERABILITY.

If any provision of this Act is held invalid, the remainder of the Act shall not be affected.

TITLE VI: GENERAL PROVISIONS

SEC. 601. AUTHORIZATION OF APPROPRIATIONS.

There are authorized to be appropriated $25,000,000,000 for fiscal years 2027 through 2032 to carry out this Act, with funds remaining available until expended.

SEC. 602. EFFECTIVE DATE.

This Act shall take effect 30 days after the date of its enactment.

🚨 Data Centers in Chester & Berks Counties: Smart Infrastructure or Speculative Gamble on Power Prices?

After two decades restructuring data centers, I’ve watched the industry reinvent itself every 10–15 years with brutal efficiency — from mainframes in the ‘80s, to colocation in the ‘90s, multi-tenant servers in the 00's, hyperscale clouds in the 10s, and now the AI data center boom.

Each wave doesn’t replace the last because the old tech failed. It gets replaced because the economics and applications change.

That’s exactly why I’m watching the surge of data center proposals in Chester and Berks Counties with deep caution.

These projects aren’t just infrastructure plays. They’re high-stakes bets on two volatile things staying true for decades:

1. Cheap, reliable electricity
2. Low-latency fiber connectivity

Southeastern Pennsylvania looks great on paper. Microsoft’s 20-year deal to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 (targeted for 2027) promises 835 MW of carbon-free baseload power for AI. The major fiber corridor from Boston to D.C. runs right through the region.

But here’s the reality check:

PJM (our regional grid) is already seeing electricity prices climb sharply due to data center-driven demand. Forecasts show data centers could add up to 30 gigawatts of new load by 2030. Capacity auction costs are exploding — billions in extra charges being socialized across all ratepayers. Local utilities like PECO are facing massive interconnection requests that could double peak demand.

Aging transmission lines and substations weren’t built for this kind of always-on, concentrated load. Upgrades cost billions and take years. When developers don’t fully cover them, the cost lands on families and small businesses.

Residents in East [NAME], East Whiteland, and other towns are already pushing back — concerned about grid strain, noise, water use, and the risk that today’s “cheap power” deal becomes tomorrow’s regret.

The fiber advantage is real, but latency-sensitive workloads can (and will) move if power costs rise faster than expected. And they will.

The next industry restructuring cycle is already coming. AI training and inference today could look like yesterday’s commodity servers once the next efficiency breakthrough or location arbitrage appears.

Bottom line: Application still determines everything.

A Wall Street bank can pay premium power prices near New York because microseconds mean billions of dollars. The same rates would kill the economics of AI cat videos or cheap cloud storage.
Unless developers can clearly explain — with real transparency — exactly what high-value workloads will live in these facilities, and why they must be here (not in cheaper-power regions), this isn’t sustainable infrastructure.

It’s real estate speculation on electricity prices and fiber proximity… and our communities could be left holding the bag when the economics shift.

I’m not against data centers done right.

Done right means:

1. Transparent economics
2. Developers paying 100% upfront for grid upgrades
3. Clear, long-term applications that justify the power draw for decades
4. Real answers to tough questions: Who pays if prices double? 5. What happens when the next tech wave hits?

Chester and Berks have a rare opportunity with the TMI restart and the fiber route. Let’s not waste it on speculative projects that treat our grid and communities like a commodity.

Local officials and residents should demand clarity now. The towns that insist on it will thrive in the next restructuring. The ones that don’t may end up with higher electric bills, reliability issues, and regret.

What do you think? Should we welcome every data center proposal, or demand stronger guarantees first?
